sub: Named after “the iron” (al-ḥadīd) Allah sent down, in ayah 25
theme: A call to believers to spend in Allah’s cause, because wealth is only on loan from Him. Real faith is not just words: it means a humble heart and sincere sacrifice.
story: Revealed in Madinah, probably in the years between the Battle of Uḥud and the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah. The young Muslim state was surrounded by enemies, and it needed its people’s wealth as much as their lives.

So the surah makes a strong appeal to spend. Wealth belongs to Allah and passes from hand to hand. Giving when Islam is weak counts for more than giving once it is winning. Faith that holds back is hollow.

Believers are also warned not to let their hearts harden like earlier communities. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite this surah and the others opening with Allah’s glorification before sleeping, saying one ayah in them is better than a thousand.

sections.title: Allah owns and knows everything; so believe, and spend what He entrusted
sections.meaning: Everything in the heavens and earth glorifies Allah. He owns it all, gives life and death, and knows every secret. So believe in Him and His Messenger ﷺ, and spend from wealth that is only in your hands for a while. Those who gave before the conquest rank higher, but all are promised good.
points: Everything glorifies Him; He is the First, the Last, the Manifest, the Hidden
Creator in six days, with you wherever you are, knows every heart
Believe and spend; why not believe, when the Messenger ﷺ calls you?
Why not spend? Givers before the conquest rank higher; all promised good
Who will lend Allah a goodly loan? He multiplies it
sections.matters: It shows who is asking before saying what He asks. The One who owns the heavens and earth, and inherits them, asks you to spend what He lent you. That turns giving from a loss into a loan to Allah.
sections.story: Reportedly, ayah 7 came about the hard expedition of Tabūk, and ayah 10 about Abū Bakr, the first to spend his wealth for the Prophet ﷺ. The “conquest” in ayah 10 is either Makkah or the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyah.
explained: Sabbaḥa: everything in the heavens and earth declares Allah free of every flaw. He owns it all. He is al-Awwal and al-Ākhir, with nothing before or after Him, aẓ-Ẓāhir and al-Bāṭin, above all yet hidden from the senses. He knows what enters the earth and what rises to the sky, and He is with you by His knowledge.

So believe, and spend. The wealth you hold passed to you from others and will pass on again; in the end everything returns to Allah. Giving when Islam was weak ranks higher than giving after victory, yet every giver is promised Paradise. And spending is a “goodly loan” that Allah repays many times over.
teaches: Your wealth is on loan from Allah; spend it while it is still in your hands.
Giving when it is hard counts for more than giving when it is easy.
When doubts creep in, recite ayah 3: the First, the Last, the Manifest, the Hidden.
Allah is with you wherever you are, and sees everything you do.
sections.hook: It opens with sabbaḥa, as do Al-Ḥashr and Aṣ-Ṣaff. Ayah 7 says “believe… spend”; then two questions open wa mā lakum: why not believe (8), why not spend (10).

sections.title: Believers walk in light, hypocrites are walled out; soften your hearts now
sections.meaning: On the Day, believers walk with light ahead of them. Hypocrites beg to borrow it and are sent back; a wall shuts them out. Then believers are asked: isn’t it time your hearts humbled? Don’t harden like those given Scripture before. Givers and true believers get their reward and their light.
points: Believers’ light runs ahead of them and on their right
Hypocrites beg for light; a wall with a door divides them
“Weren’t we with you?” Yes, but you doubted; no ransom now
Time for hearts to humble; Allah revives dead earth
Givers’ loans multiplied; believers are the truthful, with their light
sections.matters: Section 1 asked for faith and spending; this shows what they become on the Day: light. It warns that standing next to believers is not enough, and that a heart can harden slowly, so it calls believers back now.
sections.story: Ayah 16 reportedly came as a gentle rebuke: some Companions had grown relaxed, joking more, once life in Madinah became comfortable. One of them said only four years separated their Islam from this ayah. Another report links it to hypocrites.
explained: On the Day, believers walk with light running ahead and to their right, as bright as their deeds: from mountain-sized to a flickering fingertip. Hypocrites beg, “Wait, let us take some of your light.” They are told to go back and look for it, and a wall with a door rises between them: mercy inside, torment outside.

“Weren’t we with you?” they call. The reply: “Yes, but you ruined yourselves, waited for our downfall, doubted, and chased false hopes until death came.” No ransom is accepted now. Believers are asked: isn’t it time your hearts humbled? Allah revives dead earth; He can soften hard hearts. Givers and true believers get their reward and their light.
teaches: Your light on that Day is built from your deeds today.
Being among believers isn’t enough; the heart must truly believe.
Hearts harden slowly through neglect, so return to the Quran often.
A hard heart can soften, as dead earth comes back to life.
sections.hook: Three men-and-women pairs: al-muʾminīn wal-muʾmināt (12), al-munāfiqūn wal-munāfiqāt (13), al-muṣṣaddiqīn wal-muṣṣaddiqāt (18). Nūr (light) appears in 12, 13 and 19. Ayah 18 repeats 11’s goodly loan, multiplied, noble reward.

sections.title: This world withers like crops; race for Paradise; every loss is pre-written
sections.meaning: This life is play, show, boasting and piling up wealth and children, like crops that bloom, then yellow and crumble. So race for forgiveness and a Garden as wide as the sky and earth. Every hardship was written before it happened, so don’t despair over loss or boast over gain. Allah dislikes stingy boasters.
points: Life is play, show, boasting, rivalry; crops bloom, yellow, crumble
Race to forgiveness and a Garden as wide as sky and earth
Every disaster was written in a Book before it happened
So don’t grieve over loss or gloat over gain
The stingy urge stinginess; Allah is free of need
sections.matters: Two things make people forget Allah and the Hereafter: being absorbed in worldly luxury, and despair when hardship hits. This section treats both. Seeing the world as fleeting, and loss as decreed, frees you to give.
sections.story: No specific incident. When poor Emigrants worried the rich would outrank them through charity, the Prophet ﷺ taught them glorifications after each prayer. When the rich copied them, he replied with the words of ayah 21: “That is Allah’s bounty; He gives it to whom He wills.”
explained: Life’s list runs in the order people live it: laʿib (child’s play), lahw (games), zīnah (dressing up), tafākhur (boasting), takāthur (piling up wealth and children). It is like rain whose crops delight the farmers, then dry, turn yellow and crumble to straw. In the Hereafter comes either severe punishment, or forgiveness and Allah’s pleasure.

Race for a Garden as wide as sky and earth together; entering it is Allah’s bounty, not a price paid by deeds. Every loss, from drought to illness, was written before it happened. Knowing that, you won’t despair over what you missed or gloat over what you got. The arrogant boaster is also stingy, and tells others to be.
teaches: Treat this world as a crossing, not a home.
Compete with others in good deeds, not in wealth and children.
What reached you could never have missed you, and what missed you could never have reached you.
Meet joy with gratitude and grief with patience.
Don’t hold back what you owe, and don’t teach others to.
sections.hook: Iʿlamū, “know”, opens ayah 20 just as it opened 17. Its list runs laʿib, lahw, zīnah, tafākhur, takāthur. Ayah 21 ends dhū al-faḍl al-ʿaẓīm, exactly like the surah’s last ayah (29).

sections.title: Messengers brought Scripture, balance, iron; monks fell short; believers get double mercy
sections.meaning: Allah sent messengers with clear proofs, the Book and the Balance so people would live justly, and iron for strength and use. Prophethood ran through Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm’s line to ʿĪsā, whose followers were given compassion but invented a monasticism they didn’t keep properly. Believe in the Prophet ﷺ: double mercy, light and forgiveness.
points: Messengers came with proofs, Book and Balance; iron has might and benefit
Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm: prophethood and Scripture stayed in their line
ʿĪsā’s followers: compassion, and a monasticism they didn’t keep
Fear Allah, believe in His Messenger: double mercy, light, forgiveness
All bounty is in Allah’s hand; He gives whom He wills
sections.matters: It places the Prophet ﷺ at the end of one long chain of messengers, all sent for justice. It shows that devotion without faithful follow-through falls short, and it closes the surah’s call: real faith brings a double share of mercy and the light promised earlier.
sections.story: Reportedly, after ʿĪsā, kings changed the Torah and Gospel. Believers who refused were threatened, so some withdrew into towers, roamed the land, or built desert monasteries. Later generations copied them without faith. Ayat 28–29 reportedly came when some People of the Book boasted over the Muslims or envied them.
explained: Allah sent messengers with clear proofs, the Book, and al-mīzān, the Balance of justice, so people would deal fairly. He also sent down iron: strength for weapons and countless everyday uses. Through it Allah shows who will support His religion and messengers without seeing Him. He needs no help; the test is for their own good.

Prophethood and Scripture stayed in the line of Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm; some followed guidance, many didn’t. Then came ʿĪsā with the Gospel. His followers had tenderness and mercy, and took up a monasticism Allah never prescribed, then failed to keep it properly. Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger ﷺ, for two shares of mercy, light and forgiveness.
teaches: Revelation and justice go together; the Balance is for living fairly.
Support Allah’s religion even though you can’t see Him; that is the test.
Don’t add to religion what Allah didn’t prescribe, and keep what you commit to.
All bounty is in Allah’s hand; no group can claim a monopoly on it.
sections.hook: Laqad arsalnā opens ayah 25, and wa-laqad arsalnā opens 26. “Many of them are fāsiqūn” ends 26 and 27, echoing 16. Juz 27 ends here on page 541; Al-Mujādilah opens Juz 28.

groups.text: Everything glorifies Allah. He owns all, gives life and death, and is the First, the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.
He created the heavens and earth in six days, knows what enters and leaves them, is with you, and knows every heart.
Believe and spend from what He entrusted to you. Why not believe, when the Messenger ﷺ calls you out of darkness into light?
Why not spend, when everything returns to Allah? Early givers rank higher, all are promised good, and every loan to Allah is multiplied.
Believers walk with light and hear of eternal gardens. Hypocrites beg to share it, are sent back, and a wall divides them.
“Weren’t we with you?” Yes, in body, but you doubted and were deceived. No ransom is taken; the Fire is your home.
Isn’t it time believers’ hearts humbled, unlike those given Scripture whose hearts hardened? Allah revives dead earth.
Charity-givers’ loans are multiplied. Believers are the truthful and the martyrs, with reward and light; deniers go to Hellfire.
Worldly life is play, show, boasting and rivalry, like crops that bloom, yellow and crumble. The Hereafter holds punishment or forgiveness.
So race for forgiveness and a Garden as wide as sky and earth. Entering it is Allah’s bounty.
Every disaster was written before it happened, so you don’t despair over loss or gloat over gain.
Allah dislikes boasters who are stingy and tell others to be. Whoever turns away, Allah needs no one.
Messengers came with proofs, the Book and the Balance for justice, and iron for strength and use, testing who supports Allah.
Prophethood ran through Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm’s line to ʿĪsā. His followers had mercy but invented a monasticism they didn’t keep.
Fear Allah and believe in His Messenger ﷺ for double mercy and light. All bounty is in Allah’s hand alone.

1.explain: Sabbaḥa: everything in the heavens and earth, living or not, declares Allah free of every flaw. Al-ʿAzīz: all things submit to Him. Al-Ḥakīm: wise in what He creates and commands.

2.explain: He alone owns the heavens and earth and runs them. He brings to life and causes death, and nothing is beyond His power.

3.explain: Al-Awwal: nothing before Him. Al-Ākhir: nothing after Him. Aẓ-Ẓāhir: nothing above Him. Al-Bāṭin: hidden from the senses, yet knowing every hidden thing. The Prophet ﷺ used these four names in a bedtime supplication.

4.explain: Created in six days, then rose over the Throne as befits Him. He knows what sinks into the earth and grows out, what descends and what rises, like deeds. He is with you by His knowledge, seeing all you do.

5.explain: His dominion is repeated: He owns this life and the next. Every matter returns to Him, and He will sort the good from the bad and repay each.

6.explain: He merges night into day and day into night, lengthening one and shortening the other through the seasons. He knows dhāt aṣ-ṣudūr: the secrets and beliefs hidden in every chest.

7.explain: Believe, and keep believing. Mustakhlafīn: either trustees of wealth that is really Allah’s, or successors who received it from others and will pass it on. So spend; a great reward awaits.
7.why: Reportedly revealed about the expedition of hardship, Tabūk, with “those who believe and spend” pointing to ʿUthmān.

8.explain: What stops you believing, when the Messenger ﷺ himself calls you, with clear proofs? Allah took your covenant: either when all souls said “Yes, You are our Lord”, or through the pledge to the Prophet ﷺ.

9.explain: He sends down clear ayat, the Quran, to His servant Muhammad ﷺ, to bring you out of the darkness of ignorance and disbelief into the light of faith. Raʾūf, Raḥīm: kinder to you than a mother to her child.

10.explain: Mīrāth: all you own will leave your hands and return to Allah, so spend it now. Those who gave and fought before al-fatḥ (Makkah’s conquest, or Ḥudaybiyah) rank higher, yet both groups are promised Paradise.
10.why: Reportedly revealed about Abū Bakr, the first to accept Islam and the first to spend his wealth on the Prophet ﷺ.

11.explain: Qarḍ ḥasan: spending sincerely for Allah, from lawful wealth, given gladly. Allah calls it a loan though the wealth is His. Reportedly, when this came down, Abū ad-Daḥdāḥ gave Allah his garden of 600 date palms.

12.explain: Their light runs ahead of them and on their right, on the way across the Ṣirāṭ, each as bright as their deeds. Or “on their right” means their records in their right hands. Good news: gardens forever, the great success.

13.explain: Unẓurūnā: “wait for us.” The hypocrites’ light is either never given or put out at the bridge. They are told to go back and seek light. A wall (sūr) rises: mercy on the believers’ side, torment on theirs.

14.explain: “Weren’t we with you,” praying and fasting? “Yes, but you ruined yourselves with hypocrisy, waited for disaster to hit us, doubted, and false hopes fooled you until death came.” Al-gharūr, the Deceiver, is Shayṭān.

15.explain: No fidyah (ransom) is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers, not even an earth full of gold. The Fire is their mawlā: the place that fits them and holds them close.

16.explain: Alam yaʾni: hasn’t the time come? Takhshaʿa: for hearts to soften and submit to the Quran. Don’t be like those given Scripture before, the Jews and Christians: long years passed, their hearts hardened, and many became fāsiqūn, defiantly disobedient.
16.why: Reportedly a gentle rebuke to Companions who grew relaxed and joked more once life in Madinah was comfortable; one said it came four years after they accepted Islam. Another report says it was about hypocrites who kept asking Salmān for the Torah’s wonders.

17.explain: Just as Allah brings dead, dry earth back to life with rain, He can bring hard hearts back to life with the Quran, and raise the dead. The signs are clear for anyone who thinks.

18.explain: Al-muṣṣaddiqīn: men and women who give charity (another reading: who believe). They lend Allah a goodly loan, given sincerely, and it is multiplied from ten to seven hundred times and more, with a noble reward in Paradise.

19.explain: Believers in Allah and His messengers are the ṣiddīqūn, the truthful. Either they are also the martyrs, or a new sentence starts: the martyrs are with their Lord, with their reward and light. Deniers belong to al-jaḥīm, the Blaze.

20.explain: The list follows life’s stages: laʿib (child’s play), lahw (games), zīnah (show), tafākhur (boasting), takāthur (more wealth and children). Al-kuffār here means farmers who admire the crop, or disbelievers who admire the world. Matāʿ al-ghurūr: enjoyment that deceives.

21.explain: Sābiqū: race, before illness or death stops you, and compete in good deeds. The Garden is as wide as sky and earth joined together. No one enters by deeds alone, only by Allah’s bounty.

22.explain: Muṣībah: any hardship, on the earth (drought, failed crops) or in yourselves (illness, losing a child). All of it is written in the Preserved Tablet before Allah creates it, and recording it all is easy for Him.

23.explain: Allah told you this so you don’t grieve over what you missed or exult arrogantly over what you got. Everyone feels joy and sadness; make joy gratitude and sadness patience. Mukhtāl fakhūr: the self-admiring boaster.

24.explain: These boasters withhold what they owe and urge others to hold back too. Whoever turns from obeying Allah only harms himself: al-Ghanī needs no one, and al-Ḥamīd deserves all praise.

25.explain: Bayyināt: miracles and clear proofs. Al-mīzān: justice, or the actual scale. Anzalnā al-ḥadīd: Allah brought iron into being, with baʾs shadīd (weapons) and benefits (tools). Bil-ghayb: supporting Him without seeing Him. The surah is named from this ayah.

26.explain: Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm are named because every later prophet and every revealed Book came from their descendants. Some of those they were sent to were guided; many were fāsiqūn, defying Allah.

27.explain: Raʾfah and raḥmah: tenderness and mercy. Rahbāniyyah: giving up marriage and living in cells. Either they invented it seeking Allah’s pleasure, or Allah prescribed only seeking His pleasure. Most didn’t keep it; the believers among them were rewarded.
27.why: Reportedly, kings after ʿĪsā altered the Torah and Gospel and threatened believers who refused. Some withdrew into towers, roamed the land, or built desert monasteries. Later generations copied the lifestyle without their faith.

28.explain: Either addressed to believers in Mūsā and ʿĪsā, or to all believers. Kiflayn: two shares, one for the earlier faith and one for faith in Muhammad ﷺ. Plus a light to walk by, on the Ṣirāṭ or as guidance.
28.why: Reportedly, when “they will be given their reward twice” (28:54) came down, some People of the Book boasted over the Companions, or claimed even their non-believers matched the Muslims. This ayah answered with a double share for those who believe in the Prophet ﷺ.

29.explain: Li-allā yaʿlama: the lā adds emphasis; it means “so that they know.” People of the Book who reject the Prophet ﷺ cannot restrict Allah’s bounty to themselves. It is in His hand alone.
29.why: Reportedly, some People of the Book envied the believers. Another report: some Jews expected the coming prophet to be one of them, and rejected him when he came from the Arabs.
